title: Notion AI chat transcripts exposed in Fireworks AI breach
content:
All security advisories
Updates
- Investigating In addition to previously notifying the impacted customers, on November 12 we reported exposed third-party API keys found in affected user messages to the vendors that issued them.
- Investigating On 11 November, we revoked exposed Notion API keys that were found in affected user messages during our investigation.
Fireworks AI incident
Investigating
Updated version: 10 November 2026.
This post informs you about the recent Fireworks AI incident and how it’s impacting <1% of Notion workspaces. For the latest on the Fireworks AI incident, please see their official updates here.
We have contacted our customers who were affected by the Fireworks incident. If you haven’t heard from us, we haven’t identified your workspace as affected, and no action is needed right now. Our investigation is ongoing. If we determine that your workspace was impacted, we will contact you directly.
What happened and how we addressed it:
Upon analysis of the dataset Fireworks AI gave us on 8 November, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable. “Unattributable” means the chats weren’t labelled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results. Beyond what’s in the chat transcript itself, there’s no information tying the chat back to workspaces, users or companies.
No other Notion features were affected, and we continue to monitor this incident.
What is Fireworks AI and how we used them: Fireworks is one of the most used global AI infrastructure platforms powering tens of thousands of customers and used by hundreds of thousands of developers. We used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights, and we used them as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product. The Insights feature has been disabled as we investigate this incident, and we are no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.
What we recommend for affected customers: Affected customers are able to retrieve and review the impacted data securely inside their workspace, with instructions sent via email. We also recommend that affected customers treat this data as if it were exposed. If those with affected workspaces have pasted sensitive information, passwords, API keys or other credentials into Notion AI during the timeframe of the incident, rotate them.
We will update this page as we learn more.
We take your privacy and the security of your data seriously. Even though this was not a breach of our systems, keeping your data safe is fundamental to using Notion for your life’s work. It is our mission to make sure this never happens again. We will raise the standard for how your data is protected.
On 10 November, we updated this post for style and clarity in response to customer questions and feedback. No changes have been made to previously reported facts. View the previous version of this article.
Originally published

report.summary: A breach at AI vendor Fireworks AI exposed Notion AI chat transcripts from under 1% of workspaces, prompting Notion to disable Insights and revoke leaked API keys.
report.background: Notion AI runs on a chain of third-party model providers, and Fireworks AI was one of them: a widely used inference platform that also handled background classification jobs. Like many SaaS companies adding AI features, Notion sent customer prompt data to that vendor for processing and evaluation, governed by a subprocessor agreement rather than direct customer consent. That arrangement is now standard across the industry, but it concentrates risk: a single vendor incident can surface data from thousands of downstream products at once. Regulators in the EU and UK increasingly require disclosure of such subprocessors and strict limits on how prompt data is retained or reused. Meanwhile, enterprises have been demanding no-training guarantees and data-residency options before rolling out AI assistants internally, and incidents like this give procurement teams concrete ammunition.
key_points: Notion used Fireworks AI to run classification jobs for a feature called Insights, which helps customers understand their own AI usage. The dataset Fireworks handed over on 8 November contained Notion AI chat transcripts from those jobs. Notion says that for most affected workspaces the transcripts were 'unattributable' — no names, workspace IDs, or tool call results attached.

The exposure touched fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces. Notion says it has contacted every affected customer directly and that anyone who has not heard from the company was not identified as impacted, although the investigation is still ongoing and more notifications remain possible.

Notion's response was swift and broad. It disabled the Insights feature, stopped serving open-weight models through Fireworks entirely, revoked exposed Notion API keys found inside affected messages on 11 November, and reported third-party API keys to their issuing vendors the next day.

The most practical danger is secrets left in prompts. Notion advises affected customers to treat the data as exposed and to rotate any passwords, API keys, or credentials pasted into Notion AI during the incident window — a reminder that chat logs are a common hiding place for credentials.

Notion stresses this was not a breach of its own systems, framing it as third-party vendor risk. Legally that distinction matters, but for customers the outcome is the same: their text left Notion's perimeter and ended up in someone else's dataset.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a supply-chain warning. Every assistant built on a third-party inference provider inherits that provider's security posture, and 'we only sent anonymised classification data' is a thin defence once transcripts exist in someone else's storage. Expect enterprise buyers to demand subprocessor lists, prompt-retention limits, and contractual breach notification windows. For developers, the lesson is operational: stop treating prompts as ephemeral, add secret scanning and DLP before text leaves your application, and never let a model vendor retain raw user content by default. For regular users, the practical takeaway is simpler — anything typed into an AI assistant may be stored, logged, and processed elsewhere, so passwords and API keys should never go into a chat box, and any that did should be rotated now.
report.tools: To follow up: watch Fireworks AI's official incident updates and Notion's security advisories page. For teams wanting to reduce third-party exposure, self-hosted inference via vLLM or Ollama keeps prompt data in-house, while LiteLLM and similar gateways add logging controls and redaction in front of external providers. For secret hygiene, run gitleaks or TruffleHog over repositories and logs, and use Microsoft Presidio or Nightfall to detect credentials and PII before prompts are sent to any model vendor.
